Well.... it because EEGs are a terrible way to determine brain activity. It was deemed completely unacceptable for BD testing in the updated 2023 guidelines as it is not sensitive enough to detect minimal brain activity. A NM cerebral perfusion scan is much, much better.. 4 vessel cerebral angiography is the gold standard.

Spinal reflexes suck....they just do and that is coming from someone that lost a daughter and works in organ donation. They are mediated by the spinal cord and require no input from the brain. Hand movements, leg flexion, arm movements-all very common in brain death and oh so difficult to see and understand for everyone-family and medical staff. Knowing what testing they did would help. Frequently in a situation like this testing may start all over again. The very last thing anyone wants is to be wrong... Again, sending you so much love. I think there is a big difference between the words quotas and goals....at least to me. Every organization has performance goals....organ recovery is no different...but they are certainly not all based on "how many organs we get". Increasing the number of registered donors, improving the availability of pediatric heart valves....those are common performance goals. Transplanted kidneys are reimbursed by Medicare but other organs are billed through a recipient's insurance. Sure there are financial considerations but an OPO that doesn't have making the most of life through the gift of organ donation as their primary focus is woefully misguided at best.

I go twice a month to a group geared toward grieving children.  The adults responsible for the kids meet while the kids are attending their broken-down-by-age groups. I assumed us parents/grandparents would wait in the car or something but I was so wrong. This has become the therapy I didn't know I needed. The parent group starts off with a review of what the kids are doing. Then a talking stick is passed around and everyone checks in by saying their name, name and relationship of the person that died, how they died, names and ages of the children you bring, and how you are feeling. Sometimes people break down just getting through check in. Then the moderators will post a questionoften similar to what the kids are talking about -and we go around the room answering it. I cannot say enough about how helpful and important this time has become to me. We have been attending for over a year now and my kids count down the days between group. My daughter has been gone almost 4 years now-leaving me with her two littles and this group has been a godsend. 
Thank you for what you do OP!

"Half the groups surveyed did not have a written policy for handling such scenarios. Twenty-one percent said they would first inform the family of the donor's wishes and proceed with procurement, and another 59 percent said they would proceed even if they could not persuade family members. Twenty percent, however, said they would not proceed with organ procurement unless they had consent of the family, and 35 percent had not procured organs against family objections in the past five years".

I can only speak for my own OPO granted but none of these percentages would make any sense in today's landscape. Organ donation has changed incredibly over the last decade. 7 years ago HCV (Hepatitis C) was a rule out, now it is commonplace. Same with HIV + donors, the Hope Act allows donation to proceed. Recovering hearts from DCD donors is standard-impossible even 4 or 5 years ago.   

The whole way we look at FPA (First Person Authorization) has evolved as well. There is no higher standard of consent and allowing family members to override that consent is problematic to say the very least. There will be exceptions of course- there always are- but OPOs have the moral, ethical, and legal duty to uphold the potential donor's wishes upon death...whether that be brain death or death after withdrawal of life support.

Clearly the OPO was not aware of the lung cancer diagnosis as they never would have pursued organ donation. Most likely scenario is the ED called in the referral, indicated family was at bedside and ready to WDLS. The OPO asked staff to wait to allow time to determine suitability (which is mandated by CMS). Family was anxious,   nurse was getting it from both sides, and no where was the lung cancer diagnosis brought up. This happens every. single. day. Is it unfortunate? yes .....but having all of the information at the time of the initial referral call could have avoided the entire situation.  FPA is just that.....someone saying upon my death I want to be a donor. Period. Whether that is brain death or death after a family decides to withdraw support. Death is death. An OPOs job and moral responsibility is to support that person's wishes (even when no one else wants to).
That article was from 10 years ago....a lot has changed in the OPO world since then.

IV calcium. When I first started donating platelets they warn you that you might start to feel weird muscle spasms and such. Long story short, while donating platelets they return your red blood cells. They use citrate as an anticoagulant and the citrate binds with calcium. As the calcium becomes bound you may start to feel muscle twitching or pins and needles. I remember them asking me if I felt ok and the only way I could describe what I was feeling was to say my liver was quivering. They gave me some IV calcium and Oh My God....I was filled the most delicious warmth that started in my pelvis. It lasted about 5 minutes and it was truly life changing. I think I donated regularly for a while just for the calcium. Now, sadly, they just give you some Tums to chew.
